rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the cup was found, the brothers called the episode astonishing, blamed Rachel’s sons, and Benjamin answered that they had lost Joseph and now accused him; he said whoever planted the cup had planted their returned goods too.
rows.anchor: هذه الواقعة عجيبة أن راحيل ولدت ولدين لصين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers meant that Joseph and his brother shared a thieving disposition because they had a different mother, while they themselves disavowed that character.
rows.anchor: وكان غرضهم من هذا الكلام أنا لسنا على طريقته ولا على سيرته

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: One explanation says Joseph stole and broke the idols worshipped by his maternal grandfather, at his mother’s request, hoping he would abandon idol worship.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير : كان جده أبو أمه كافرا يعبد الأوثان فأمرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Joseph took food from his father’s table and gave it to the poor.
rows.anchor: أنه كان يسرق الطعام من مائدة أبيه ويدفعه إلى الفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports say Joseph took a young gazelle or a chicken from his father and gave it to a needy person.
rows.anchor: وقيل سرق عناقا من أبيه ودفعه إلى المسكين وقيل دجاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s aunt, who loved him and wished to keep him, tied Isaac’s treasured belt around him, claimed he stole it, and used their enslavement rule to retain him.
rows.anchor: وكان من حكمهم بأن من سرق يسترق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi also allows that the brothers simply lied about Joseph out of lasting anger; the incident shows an envious heart is never cleansed of rancor.
rows.anchor: وهذه الواقعة تدل على أن قلب الحاسد لا يطهر عن الغل ألبتة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes the feminine pronoun in “asarrhā” as an anticipatory pronoun explained by “you are worse in station”; the explained clause is treated as a phrase or word, a feminine noun.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : فأسرها إضمار على شريطة التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Masud’s reading uses the masculine “asarra,” referring to the saying or speech.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة ابن مسعود { فأسر } بالتذكير

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali objects that an anticipatory pronoun explained by a clause must belong to that same clause; here the explanation is separate, so the construction is unsuitable.
rows.anchor: الوجه الأول : قال الإضمار على شريطة التفسير يكون على ضربين

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: He further argues that “you are worse in station” says Yusuf spoke those words; claiming he only thought them would make the verse falsely report his speech.
rows.anchor: وذلك يدل على أنه ذكر هذا الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi calls Abu Ali’s objection weak: accepting two known types of anticipatory pronoun does not rule out a third, and Yusuf could have said the words secretly.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن هذا الطعن ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “asarrhā” can refer to the brothers’ reply: Yusuf kept his response to their accusation in himself and did not reveal it then.
rows.anchor: والوجه الثاني : وهو أن الضمير في قوله : { فأسرها } عائد إلى الإجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may instead refer to their statement or its subject: Yusuf privately retained how the theft occurred, without explaining that it warranted no blame.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أيضا أن يكون إضمارا للمقالة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says Joseph was punished three times: imprisonment, prolonged imprisonment after asking the cupbearer to remember him, and his brothers’ later accusation that his brother had stolen before.
rows.anchor: روي عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أنه قال عوقب يوسف عليه السلام ثلاث مرات لأجل همه بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You are worse in station” means worse before God because they wronged their brother, disobeyed and deceived their father, sold Joseph, and still accused him after many years.
rows.anchor: أنتم شر منزلة عند الله تعالى لما أقدمتم عليه من ظلم أخيكم وعقوق أبيكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows whether the accusation they described warrants blame; none of the reported explanations of Joseph’s theft entails reproach, and his act was for God’s approval.
rows.anchor: يريد أن سرقة يوسف كانت رضا لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After claiming the thief must be enslaved, the brothers switch to intercession: pardon or ransom was also permitted, so they ask the ruler to accept one of them instead.
rows.anchor: أحبوا موافقته والعدول إلى طريقة الشفاعة فإنهم وإن كانوا قد اعترفوا أن حكم الله تعالى في السارق أن يستعبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their description of Jacob as an old father may refer to age or to great standing and religion; his stature is offered as a reason for pardon.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون في القدر والدين ، وإنما ذكروا ذلك لأن كونه ابنا لرجل كبير القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Take one of us in his place” can mean take one as a slave, or hold one as security until they deliver ransom.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون المراد على طريق الاستبعاد ويحتمل أن يكون المراد على طريق الرهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We see you as beneficent” may mean they would regard him as beneficent if he freed Benjamin.
rows.anchor: إنا نراك من المحسنين لو فعلت ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may instead be recalling Joseph’s prior generosity: he honored them, gave abundant provisions, and returned their payment.
rows.anchor: حيث أكرمتنا وأعطيتنا البذل الكثير وحصلت لنا مطلوبنا على أحسن الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says famine drove Egyptians to sell themselves for food; after most became his slaves, Joseph freed them all, so the brothers ask him to free Benjamin too.
rows.anchor: وكانوا يبيعون أنفسهم منه فصار ذلك سببا لصيرورة أكثر أهل مصر عبيدا له ثم إنه أعتق الكل

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj parses “an” as accusative after an omitted “min”: Joseph seeks refuge from taking one person for another’s offense.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : موضع ( أن ) نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says taking anyone except the person found with the property would make them unjust by harming someone for another’s offense.
rows.anchor: أي لقد تعديت وظلمت إن آذيت إنسانا بجرم صدر عن غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi raises the objection that Joseph’s elaborate deception, false accusation, and imprisonment intensified Jacob’s grief despite Joseph’s prophethood and knowledge of the consequences.
rows.anchor: فكيف يجوز من يوسف عليه السلام مع رسالته الإقدام على هذا التزوير والترويج وإيذاء الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that God may have commanded Joseph to intensify Jacob’s trial and prohibited pardon or taking a substitute, as God commanded Moses’ companion to kill someone who otherwise would have transgressed.
rows.anchor: لعله تعالى أمره بذلك تشديدا للمحنة على يعقوب ونهاه عن العفو والصفح وأخذ البدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After offering their utmost and being refused, the brothers lose hope; they withdraw from other people to consult over a difficult return made worse by their oath, past suspicion, their father’s age, hunger at home, and the shame of returning without Benjamin.
rows.anchor: فعند هذا قال تعالى : { فلما * استيأسوا منه خلصوا نجيا }

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi reports Ibn Kathir read “istayāsū” without hamza, as in the reading of “istayʾasa” in 12:110.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي روي عن ابن كثير استياسوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic has yaʾisa/yāʾasu alongside yaʾisa/yaʾyasu; forming istayʾasa shifts the middle radical to the first position, then the hamza is softened.
rows.anchor: وفي ييئس لغتان يئس وييأس مثل حسب ويحسب ومن قال استيأس قلب العين إلى موضع الفاء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the added sīn and tā intensify the meaning, as in “istaʿṣama” in 12:32.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : استيأسوا يئسوا

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi explains the root of “khalasa” as becoming free of foreign admixture.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : يقال خلص الشيء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj interprets “khalasū” as separating by themselves, without their brother.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج خلصوا أي انفردوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other exegetes understand “khalasū” as separating from outsiders, which Razi calls the more apparent explanation.
rows.anchor: قال الباقون تميزوا عن الأجانب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says “najiyy” can mean a person engaged in confidential conversation or the act of confidential conversation, as “najwā” can mean those conversing privately.
rows.anchor: النجي على معنيين يكون بمعنى المناجي كالعشير والسمير بمعنى المعاشر والمسامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi’s best explanation is that the brothers became wholly absorbed in private consultation, as though they themselves had become the conversation.
rows.anchor: وأحسن الوجوه أن يقال : إنهم تمحضوا تناجيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their eldest” is explained either as Reuben, eldest by age, or Judah, greatest in judgment and the brother who stopped them from killing Joseph.
rows.anchor: فقيل المراد كبيرهم في السن وهو روبيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says Judah’s anger made pregnant hearers miscarry and raised the hair on his body; he told his brothers to handle the Egyptians while he confronted the king.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : لما قال يوسف عليه السلام : { معاذ الله أن نأخذ إلا من وجدنا متاعنا عنده }

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The same report says Joseph had a young son touch Judah to calm him, then pulled Judah down when he was about to shout; after the failed plea the brothers recalled their oath and their prior suspicion over Joseph.
rows.anchor: فقال يوسف عليه السلام لابن صغير له مسه فمسه فذهب غضبه وهم أن يصيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers judge returning to Jacob and reporting events accurately to be best; the eldest who stayed in Egypt—identified by some as Reuben—apparently told them to go.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا القول قاله ذلك الكبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They concluded Benjamin likely took the cup because it was in a place only they could enter; unlike the returned goods, nobody admitted placing the cup in his pack, so they spoke from probability rather than certainty.
rows.anchor: فلما شاهدوا أنهم أخرجوا الصواع من رحله غلب على ظنونهم أنه هو الذي أخذ الصواع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “your son stole” reports the king and his attendants’ judgment, as Qur’anic statements may describe what someone believes of himself.
rows.anchor: في قول الملك وأصحابه ومثله كثير في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, what appeared like theft may be called theft by analogy, as one similar thing may be named by the other.
rows.anchor: أن ابنك ظهر عليه ما يشبه السرقة ومثل هذا الشيء يسمى سرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further answer is that the brothers were not prophets then and may have made a reckless claim after seeing evidence that seemed to implicate Benjamin.
rows.anchor: أن القوم ما كانوا أنبياء في ذلك الوقت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to read “suriqa” with gemination, meaning Benjamin was accused of theft; Razi says this does not resolve the problem unless the first reading is rejected, so an earlier explanation remains necessary.
rows.anchor: أن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما كان يقرأ { إن ابنك سرق }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We testified only to what we knew” shows testimony differs from knowledge; the Prophet’s instruction to testify when knowledge is like the sun likewise presupposes the distinction.
rows.anchor: فمعناه ظاهر لأنه يدل على أن الشهادة غير العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Testimony is a mental judgment, called inner speech by theologians; saying “I testify” merely reports testimony and is not testimony itself.
rows.anchor: الشهادة عبارة عن الحكم الذهني وهو الذي يسميه المتكلمون بكلام النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of not guarding the unseen is that they saw the cup taken from Benjamin’s pack but could not know the hidden reality, which only God knows.
rows.anchor: أنا قد رأينا أنهم أخرجوا الصواع من رحله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says the cup may have been planted in Benjamin’s belongings at night, since “the unseen” can mean night in some dialects.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة معناه : لعل الصواع دس في متاعه بالليل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Qatada explain that they did not know Benjamin would steal; had they known, they would not have taken him to the ruler or pledged his return.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد والحسن وقتادة : وما كنا نعلم أن ابنك يسرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says Jacob asked how the king knew Israelite theft law; the brothers replied that they had described the rule before this incident, without knowing it would occur.
rows.anchor: نقل أن يعقوب عليه السلام قال لهم : فهب أنه سرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that Jacob may have regarded enslavement for theft as a rule applicable only when the victim was Muslim, and therefore objected to telling a king he thought was an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: لعله كان ذلك الحكم مخصوصا بما إذا كان المسروق منه مسلما فلهذا أنكر ذكر هذا الحكم عند الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify the town as Egypt; others identify a village at its edge where the theft and search were discussed.
rows.anchor: والأكثرون اتفقوا على أن المراد من هذه القرية مصر وقال قوم ، بل المراد منه قرية على باب مصر جرى فيها حديث السرقة والتفتيش

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Most explain “ask the town” by ellipsis for its people; Abu Ali al-Farisi says rejecting this familiar Arabic metonymy is like denying obvious necessities and perceptions.
rows.anchor: وهذا النوع من المجاز مشهور في لغة العرب قال أبو علي الفارسي ودافع جواز هذا في اللغة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الأنباري
rows.claim: Al-Anbari offers a literal miraculous reading: ask the town, caravan, walls, and other objects, which God could make speak to confirm the brothers’ truthfulness.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر الأنباري المعنى : اسأل القرية والعير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation treats “ask heaven and earth” as hyperbole meaning the truth is so manifest that no doubt remains.
rows.anchor: وفيه وجه ثالث ، وهو أن الشيء إذا ظهر ظهورا تاما كاملا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators say Canaanites traveled with the brothers and could be asked about the incident.
rows.anchor: فقال المفسرون كان قد صحبهم قوم من الكنعانيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their insistence that they are truthful does not prove itself circularly; it directs Jacob to weigh the decisive evidence they just presented.
rows.anchor: وليس غرضهم أن يثبتوا صدق أنفسهم بأنفسهم لأن هذا يجري مجرى إثبات الشيء بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob again says his sons’ souls made a matter seem good, as in Joseph’s earlier loss, but now follows this with hope God will reunite them all rather than the earlier appeal for help against their account.
rows.anchor: فذكر هذا الكلام بعينه في هذه الواقعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says the sons’ scheme was sending Benjamin with them for expected benefit, which instead brought harm contrary to their plan and God’s decree.
rows.anchor: لكنه عنى سولت لكم أنفسكم إخراج بنيامين عني والمصير به إلى مصر طلبا للمنفعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says they imagined Benjamin had stolen when he had not.
rows.anchor: وقيل : بل المعنى سولت لكم أنفسكم أمرا خيلت لكم أنفسكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Reuben threatened to scream so loudly that pregnant women in Egypt would miscarry if forced to leave; Joseph let him stay, and Jacob lamented losing another son on each trip.
rows.anchor: فقال أتركوني وإلا صحت صيحة لا تبقى بمصر امرأة حامل إلا وتضع حملها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s expectation reflects good opinion of God after prolonged grief: he trusts that relief will soon come, perhaps because God had disclosed Joseph’s survival or shown signs of it.
rows.anchor: لما طال حزنه وبلاؤه ومحنته علم أنه تعالى سيجعل له فرجا ومخرجا عن قريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three absent sons are Joseph, Benjamin, and the eldest who remained in Egypt; this explains Jacob’s hope that God would bring them all back.
rows.anchor: فلما كان الغائبون ثلاثة لا جرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He is the All-knowing, the Wise” means God knows the realities of affairs and governs them with wisdom matching grace, kindness, mercy, and benefit.
rows.anchor: يعني هو العالم بحقائق الأمور الحكيم فيها على الوجه المطابق للفضل والإحسان والرحمة والمصلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s heart tightened after hearing his sons and he turned away from them; later he returned and spoke with them.
rows.anchor: ضاق قلبه جدا وأعرض عنهم وفارقهم ثم بالآخرة طلبهم وعاد إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: New sorrow revives old grief; Razi cites Muttammim ibn Nuwayra, whose sight of graves renewed his grief for Malik and whose reply was that sorrow awakens sorrow.
rows.anchor: وقال متمم بن نويرة : وقد لامني عند القبور على البكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another poet says a fresh wound makes an old wound hurt more, supporting the idea that new grief revives earlier pain.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر : فلم تنسني أو في المصيبات بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Benjamin resembled Joseph and shared his mother, so Jacob had been comforted by seeing him; losing him removed that consolation and intensified grief for Joseph.
rows.anchor: أن بنيامين ويوسف كانا من أم واحدة وكانت المشابهة بينهما في الصورة والصفة أكمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s loss caused the later calamities, so grief for Joseph encompassed grief for all of them.
rows.anchor: وكان الأسف عليه أسفا على الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The newer losses had discoverable causes, but Joseph’s supposed cause was known to be false and the true cause unknown; Jacob also knew the others lived but not whether Joseph did, deepening the grief.
rows.anchor: وأما واقعة يوسف فهو عليه السلام كان يعلم كذبهم في السبب الذي ذكروه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the critic who says Jacob’s lament was sinful complaint: Jacob wept but restrained lamentation, complained only to God, and thereby showed patience worthy of great praise.
rows.anchor: وكل ذلك يدل على أنه لما عظمت مصيبته وقويت محنته فإنه صبر وتجرع الغصة وما أظهر الشكاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Joseph asked Gabriel about Jacob’s grief; Gabriel likened it to that of seventy bereaved mothers and said Jacob would receive the reward of one hundred martyrs.
rows.anchor: روي أن يوسف عليه السلام سأل جبريل

rows.speaker: محمد بن علي الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir reports that God rebuked Jacob for complaining to servants and promised to replace his flesh and blood if he stopped; Jacob later said he complained only to God.
rows.anchor: روي عن محمد بن علي الباقر

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says Jacob’s brother asked what ruined his sight and bowed his back; Jacob blamed weeping for Joseph and grief for Benjamin, then asked God for his two beloved sons.
rows.anchor: وعن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( كان ليعقوب أخ مواخ )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jacob covered his raised brows with cloth; when asked, he attributed them to long years and many sorrows, then admitted a sin and sought forgiveness after God’s rebuke.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه كان يرفع حاجبيه بخرقة من الكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says Jacob displayed patience, not sinful wailing; an encounter with the Angel of Death says he came to share Jacob’s grief, and weeping itself is not a sin.
rows.anchor: وروي أن ملك الموت دخل على يعقوب عليه السلام فقال له : جئت

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet wept over his son Ibrahim, saying hearts grieve and eyes shed tears, while believers avoid words that displease God.
rows.anchor: وروي أن النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام : بكى على ولده إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grief’s inward grip is involuntary and outside moral command; sighing and tears can likewise become impossible to suppress.
rows.anchor: فاستيلاء الحزن على الإنسان ليس باختياره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reported divine rebukes reflect that what counts as a good deed for ordinary righteous people may count as a lapse for those brought especially near to God.
rows.anchor: فالمعاتبة فيها إنما كانت لأجل أن حسنات الأبرار سيئات المقربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Jacob did not know whether Joseph was alive, uncertainty drove him to return constantly to God and detach from all else; recollection of Joseph became his exceptional spiritual trial, like Abraham’s fire and the sacrifice of his son.
rows.anchor: فكان متوقفا فيه وبسبب توقفه كان يكثر الرجوع إلى الله تعالى وينقطع قلبه عن الالتفات عن كل ما سوى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the claim that only Muhammad’s community knew to say “we belong to God and return to Him”: all nations’ believers know God created and owns them and that resurrection returns them to Him, which should console them.
rows.anchor: ومن المحال أن أمة من الأمم لا يعرفون ذلك فمن عرف عند نزول بعض المصائب به أنه لا بد في العاقبة من رجوعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Yā asafā” personifies sorrow as if Jacob called it to arrive; “asaf” is grief over what has passed, and al-Layth describes an overwhelmed sufferer as asif or mutaʾassif.
rows.anchor: نداء الأسف وهو كقوله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the original form was “yā asafī”; the possessive yāʾ may become alif for ease.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : الأصل { * يا أسفى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi prefers understanding the eye’s whiteness as a figure for overwhelming weeping, since grief naturally causes tears rather than blindness; al-Wahidi transmits this explanation from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: والدليل على صحة هذا القول أن تأثير الحزن في غلبة البكاء لا في حصول العمى

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says Jacob became blind for six years until Joseph’s shirt restored his sight; proponents connect prolonged grief to continuous crying and then damage to the eye.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : لم يبصر بهما ست سنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports say Jacob retained weak vision rather than becoming wholly blind, or that his eyes never dried during eighty years apart from Joseph; one calls him the most honored servant on earth.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال : ما عمي لكنه صار بحيث يدرك إدراكا ضعيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is read “min al-ḥuzn” with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on zāy; al-Hasan reads both vowels open.
rows.anchor: أما قوله تعالى : { من الحزن } فاعلم أنه قرىء { من الحزن }

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Some distinguish ḥazan as crying and ḥuzn as the opposite of joy, while most linguists treat the two forms as synonyms; Abu Amr says accusative usage opens both vowels while nominative and genitive use ḍamma.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : واختلفوا في الحزن والحزن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kazīm” may mean one who contains his grief; Ibn Qutayba also allows the passive sense of being filled with grief, like a waterskin tightened while full, or filled with anger at his sons.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يكون بمعنى الكاظم وهو الممسك على حزنه فلا يظهره قال ابن قتيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi sees rhetorical intensification in the three noble faculties: the tongue voices sorrow, the eyes weep and whiten, and the heart is sealed full of grief.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن أشرف أعضاء الإنسان هذه الثلاثة

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit says “mā zilt,” “mā fitiʾt,” and “mā bariḥt” meaning “I kept doing it” are used only with negation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السكيت يقال : ما زلت أفعله

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba notes two dialect forms, “fatītu” and “fatiʾtu,” for forgetting or ceasing.
rows.anchor: قال ابن قتيبة يقال : ما فتيت وما فتئت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians supply an omitted negative in “tالله تفتأ”; without negation, oath language would normally contain the emphatic lām and nūn.
rows.anchor: قال النحويون وحرف النفي ههنا مضمر على معنى

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imru al-Qays’s line “I will remain seated” witnesses omission of the negative, meaning “I will not cease sitting.”
rows.anchor: عرف أن كلمة لا مضمرة وأنشدوا قول امرىء القيس :

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatada explain the brothers’ words as “you will not cease remembering Joseph”; Mujahid also says Jacob would not slacken in loving him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة لا تزال تذكره

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says the root meaning of “ḥaraḍ” is bodily and mental deterioration through grief or love; to make someone ḥaraḍ is to corrupt or inflame him against another.
rows.anchor: حكى الواحدي عن أهل المعاني أن أصل الحرض فساد الجسم والعقل للحزن والحب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling a person ḥaraḍ either omits “possessor of” or indicates that he has become the very essence of corruption; both vowelings of the adjective are read.
rows.anchor: وصف الرجل بأنه حرض إما أن يكون لإرادة أنه ذو حرض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Exegetes describe ḥaraḍ as physically and mentally ruined; Ibn Abbas tells Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq it means corrupt, sickly, and wasting away.
rows.anchor: سأل نافع بن الأزرق ابن عباس عن الحرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations call ḥaraḍ a state between life and death; Anas is reported to read it with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and sukūn on rāʾ, comparing Jacob to a dry saltwort stalk.
rows.anchor: أنه الذي يكون لا كالأحياء ولا كالأموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The family fear that grief will leave Jacob incapacitated by illness or dead, and speak to restrain his continual weeping and sorrow.
rows.anchor: حتى تصير بذلك إلى مرض لا تنتفع بنفسك معه أو تموت من الغم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath rests on what appeared likely to the speakers, not certain knowledge.
rows.anchor: إنهم بنوا هذا الأمر على الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says the speakers were probably the household group of grandchildren and servants, rather than the sons Jacob had turned away from.
rows.anchor: الأظهر أن هؤلاء ليسوا هم الإخوة الذين قد تولى عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob says he voices his intense and lesser grief to God alone; confiding pain to God places a person among the realized, as in the Prophet’s prayer seeking refuge in God from God’s displeasure.
rows.anchor: يعني أن هذا الذي أذكره لا أذكره معكم وإنما أذكره في حضرة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Bathth” means spreading; hidden sorrow is concern, while sorrow spoken aloud becomes bathth. It is more intense than grief and grief more intense than worry, since inability to hold back speech shows sorrow has mastered the person.
rows.anchor: والبث هو التفريق قال الله تعالى :

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads “ḥuznī” with both vowels open and also reports a form with both vowels ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن : { وحزنى } بفتحتين وحزني بضمتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says a visitor wondered at Jacob’s weakened body and premature aging; after God rebuked his complaint to creatures, Jacob sought forgiveness and thereafter answered with this verse.
rows.anchor: قيل : دخل على يعقوب رجل وقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says God traced Jacob’s affliction to his failure to feed a poor person who came while his household had slaughtered a sheep, and instructed him to invite the poor to a meal.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه أوحى الله إليه إنما وجدت عليكم لأنكم ذبحتم شاة فقام ببابكم مسكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A separate account says Jacob bought a servant girl with her child, sold the child, and her grief eventually made her blind.
rows.anchor: وقيل : اشترى جارية مع ولدها فباع ولدها فبكت حتى عميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I know from God what you do not know” refers to God’s mercy and generosity: relief can come unexpectedly, and Jacob expects Joseph’s return.
rows.anchor: أي أعلم من رحمته وإحسانه ما لا تعلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says the Angel of Death denied taking Joseph and pointed Jacob toward Egypt.
rows.anchor: أن ملك الموت أتاه فقال له : يا ملك الموت هل قبضت روح ابني يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob may have trusted Joseph’s dream because signs of maturity were evident, and a prophet’s dream does not fail.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : أنه علم أن رؤيا يوسف صادقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may have revealed that Jacob would reunite with Joseph without specifying when, leaving him anxious.
rows.anchor: وثالثها : لعله تعالى أوحى إليه أنه سيوصله إليه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says hearing the sons praise the ruler’s conduct made Jacob hope the ruler was Joseph, since such excellence seemed unlikely among unbelievers.
rows.anchor: قال السدي : لما أخبره بنوه بسيرة الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob knew Benjamin had not stolen and heard the ruler had not harmed him, so he inferred that the ruler might be Joseph.
rows.anchor: وخامسها : علم قطعا أن بنيامين لا يسرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Having hope of finding Joseph from these signs, Jacob gently tells his sons to search for Joseph and Benjamin.
rows.anchor: والمقام الثاني : أنه رجع إلى أولاده وتكلم معهم على سبيل اللطف

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الأنباري
rows.claim: “Taḥassus” is seeking through the senses. Al-Anbari says the usual idiom is “taḥassastu ʿan,” not “min”; here “min” substitutes for “ʿan,” or marks partitive seeking of some news.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر الأنباري يقال : تحسست عن فلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb is also read “tajassasū” with jīm; both forms occur in the reading tradition of al-Hujurat.
rows.anchor: وقرىء { تجسسوا } بالجيم كما قرىء بهما في الحجرات

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi relates “rūḥ” to a soothing breeze and to movement or vibration that a person enjoys and finds comforting.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي : الروح ما يجده الإنسان من نسيم الهواء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains “rūḥ Allah” as God’s mercy; Qatada says favor and Ibn Zayd says relief, which Razi calls close in meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : لا تيئسوا من روح الله يريد من رحمة الله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada read “rūḥ” with ḍamma, meaning mercy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وقتادة : من روح الله بالضم أي من رحمته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a believer keeps hope in God during trial and gives thanks in ease.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : إن المؤمن من الله على خير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despair of mercy entails believing God lacks power, knowledge, or generosity; each belief is unbelief, so only unbelievers despair of God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن اليأس من رحمة الله تعالى لا يحصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi raises the objection that Jacob’s consuming love of Joseph seems incompatible with knowing and wholly loving God, since one heart cannot be wholly absorbed in two objects.
rows.anchor: أن بلوغ يعقوب في حب يوسف إلى هذا الحد العظيم لا يليق إلا بمن كان غافلا عن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Objections ask why severe grief did not lead Jacob to remembrance and submission, and why he expressed sorrow in a way supposedly unfit for the devout and prophets.
rows.anchor: أن عند استيلاء الحزن الشديد عليه كان من الواجب أن يشتغل بذكر الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further objection says Jacob’s public, decades-long grief over Joseph could not remain unknown given his prophetic family, Joseph’s residence in nearby Egypt, and Jacob’s home in Syria.
rows.anchor: ومن كذلك ثم وقعت له واقعة هائلة صعبة في أعز أولاده عليه لم تبق تلك الواقعة خفية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioner asks why Joseph, once a powerful king, never sent word that he was alive, since his brothers could not stop a messenger.
rows.anchor: لم يبعث يوسف عليه السلام أحدا إلى يعقوب ويعلمه أنه في الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioner asks how Joseph could plant the cup in Benjamin’s pack and attach a false theft charge to him.
rows.anchor: كيف جاز ليوسف عليه السلام أن يضع الصاع في وعاء أخيه ثم يستخرجه منه ويلصق به تهمة السرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questioner asks why Joseph wanted Benjamin accused and imprisoned when this would worsen Jacob’s grief.
rows.anchor: كيف رغب في إلصاق هذه التهمة به وفي حبسه عند نفسه مع أنه كان يعلم أنه يزداد حزن أبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that overwhelming trial removes other thoughts, while repeatedly turning to God in prayer and supplication makes the sufferer more absorbed in God.
rows.anchor: أن مثل هذه المحنة الشديدة تزيل عن القلب كل ما سواه من الخواطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human nature remains during worldly life: Jacob sometimes voiced grief and at other times affirmed beautiful patience and sought God’s help.
rows.anchor: والجواب عن الثاني : أن الداعي الإنسانية لا تزول في الحياة العاجلة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi gives a general answer for the remaining difficulties: ordinary circumstances may explain them; otherwise extraordinary events were plausible in the age of prophets, including nearby towns failing to exchange news by normal custom.
rows.anchor: فإن كان الأول فلا إشكال ، وإن كان الثاني فنقول : كان ذلك الزمان زمان الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exegetes assume an omitted return: after Jacob told his sons to search, they returned to Egypt and entered Joseph’s presence; they use every means to achieve their aim, beginning with a plea of poverty to soften him.
rows.anchor: أن يعقوب لما قال لبنيه : { اذهبوا فتحسسوا من يوسف وأخيه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Al-ʿAzīz” means the powerful, invincible king; their family’s distress means poverty, need, many dependents, and little food.
rows.anchor: والعزيز هو الملك القادر المنيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Muzjāt” derives from gradual pushing or eking along, as wind drives clouds; they brought goods with which one barely makes time pass.
rows.anchor: معنى الإزجاء في اللغة ، الدفع قليلا قليلا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says their “muzjāt” goods were small in quantity; other commentators say they were poor in quality or both little and poor.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : البضاعة المزجاة القليلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the poor goods as rejected, inferior dirhams; other proposals include worn sacks and rope, rough Bedouin goods, green grain, dried curds, sandals and hides, arak-pulp meal, or goat wool.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما كانت دراهم رديئة لا تقبل في ثمن الطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says Egyptian dirhams bore Joseph’s image, while the brothers’ coins did not and so were unacceptable.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن دراهم مصر كانت تنقش فيها صورة يوسف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains “muzjāt” as goods used to eke out life with little, so the brothers say they have brought something barely sufficient to stretch the days.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : هي من قولهم فلان يزجي العيش

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd says inferior dirhams are called “muzjāt” because they are pushed back and rejected by people asked to accept them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد : إنما قيل للدراهم الرديئة مزجاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation calls the goods deferred from circulation: only the desperate accept them because better goods are unavailable.
rows.anchor: ببضاعة مزجاة أي مؤخرة مدفوعة عن الإنفاق لا ينفق مثلها إلا من اضطر واحتاج إليها

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi calls “muzjāt” a foreign word, perhaps Coptic, but al-Anbari rejects this because the Arabic word has a familiar derivation and morphology.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : مزجاة لغة العجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read “muzjāt” with imāla because its original form has yāʾ; the other readers use tafkhīm.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي مزجاة بالإمالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ask for a full measure by having deficient goods counted as full or inferior goods valued like good ones, and ask for the price difference as charity or leniency.
rows.anchor: والمراد أن يساهلهم إما بأن يقيم الناقص مقام الزائد أو يقيم الرديء مقام الجيد

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna says charity was lawful for prophets before Muhammad, so the brothers ask for the excess as alms.
rows.anchor: فقال سفيان بن عيينة : إن الصدقة كانت حلالا للأنبياء قبل محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most reject a request for charity as unfitting for prophets and their descendants, who avoid humiliating themselves before people and rely on God.
rows.anchor: وأنكر الباقون ذلك وقالوا حال الأنبياء وحال أولاد الأنبياء ينافي طلب الصدقة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Mujahid dislike asking God “bestow charity on me”: God does not give charity to seek a reward; one should ask Him to give or favor instead.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن ومجاهد : أنهما كرها أن يقول الرجل في دعائه

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth permits calling a supplicant a “mutaṣaddiq,” while most reject that usage; “mutaṣaddiq” otherwise means the one who gives charity.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الليث أن يقال للسائل : متصدق وأباه الأكثرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says their plea over the family’s distress brought tears to Joseph’s eyes; another says they handed him Jacob’s letter describing the family’s trials and asking that Benjamin be returned, after which Joseph revealed himself.
rows.anchor: فلما قرأ يوسف عليه السلام الكتاب لم يتمالك وعيل صبره وعرفهم أنه يوسف

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi explains “ātharaka” as God favoring Joseph; the phrase can also describe a servant whom someone prefers with special gifts.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي : يقال : آثرك إيثارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph was favored over his brothers in knowledge, forbearance, reason, virtue, beauty, and kingship.
rows.anchor: والمعنى : لقد فضلك الله علينا بالعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some infer that Joseph’s brothers were not prophets: prophethood outweighs worldly offices, so sharing that rank would make their confession of his superiority incoherent.
rows.anchor: واحتج بعضهم بهذه الآية على أن إخوته ما كانوا أنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Khāṭiʾ” denotes deliberate sin, unlike “mukhṭiʾ,” used for someone who strives to reach a legal judgment but errs.
rows.anchor: قيل الخاطىء هو الذي أتى بالخطيئة عمدا وفرق بين الخاطىء والمخطىء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators say the brothers apologize for throwing Joseph in the well, selling him, and separating him from their father.
rows.anchor: وأكثر المفسرين على أن الذي اعتذروا منه هو إقدامهم على إلقائه في الجب وبيعه

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi says they did not apologize for childhood acts before puberty, but for later hiding Joseph’s survival and failing to tell Jacob that the wolf had not eaten him.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي الجبائي : إنهم لم يعتذروا إليه من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects al-Jubbaʾi’s account as implausible: Jacob would hardly send unaccompanied prepubescent boys; even an unnecessary apology can still be fitting, as people may renew repentance after forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وهذا الكلام ضعيف من وجوه :
